## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

**February 23, 2016**

## The Top 10 Most Popular Dog Breeds in America in 2015
Yesterday, the American Kennel Club announced the results of their annual survey of the most popular dog breeds in America, and once again, the Labrador Retriever took the top spot. For 25 years in a row, the Lab has been #1 on the list, which is determined by the AKC based on the number of registrations received. In fact, 2015’s top 5 breeds are the same as last year’s list. The 6th place breed, the French Bulldog, is the biggest riser of the bunch, moving up from 9th place in 2014.
Rather than just tell you the rest of the breeds, we thought we’d show you. Here are 2015’s top 10 most popular dog breeds, starring 33 gorgeous DogWatch Dogs from across the country (and a few international ones, too)!

## 1. Labrador Retriever
Ben the Chocolate Lab from Trinidad, Shooter the Black Lab from Wichita, KS, and Maggie the Yellow Lab from Sheridan, MT.

## 2. German Shepherd
German Shepherds Sage from Illinois (with Stateline DogWatch Dealer Laurie Spain), Buzz from Michigan and Cirrus from Oregon.

## 3. Golden Retriever
Golden Retrievers Margo (L) and Kringle (R) from Massachusetts, and the “Golden Brothers” from Triad DogWatch in North Carolina.

## 4. English Bulldog
English Bulldogs Humphrey from Shoreline, WA, Oscar from DogWatch of Appalachia, and Bo from Sarasota, FL.

## 5. Beagle
Beagles Bella from Wallan, VIC, Australia, Coco from Carnegie, PA, and Winnie and Tigger from St. Louis, MO.

## 6. French Bulldog
A happy French Bulldog from DogWatch Thailand, and Frenchies Coco from Illinois and Olive from Columbus, OH.

## 7. Yorkshire Terrier
Yorkshire Terriers (or “Yorkies”) Clementine from Columbus, GA, Coco from Edina, MN, and Zeph from Montana

## The Most Popular Dog Breeds in the U.S.
U.S. News & World Report
Moving up from its previous No. 2 spot, the Chihuahua is now the most popular dog breed in the U.S. Meanwhile, the former No. 1, the Labrador retriever, has dropped to No. 3.
Across the remaining top five, the popularity of these breeds has surged over the last year: The French bulldog went from No. 6 to No. 2, retaking its 2024 position; the Yorkshire terrier climbed from No. 9 to No. 4; and the shih tzu rose from No. 8 to No. 5, also reclaiming its 2024 spot.
When looking at the rest of the top 10, here’s how things shake out:
*   The golden retriever forfeits its No. 3 spot for the first time since 2024, dropping to No. 6.  
*   After reaching No. 4 in 2025, the American pit bull terrier has dropped to the No. 8 spot it held in 2024.  
*   The German shepherd has dropped out of the top five for the first time since 2024, landing at No. 7.  
*   The goldendoodle – not a breed recognized by the American Kennel Club but treated as one for our purposes – has slipped slightly from No. 7 to No. 9.  
*   The steadfast dachshund holds firm at No. 10.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR +0.12% retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

## The Poodle's long run near the top and its recent decline
Credit: Helena Lopes / Unsplash
The Poodle ranked No. 5 among the most popular dog breeds in the U.S. for four straight years before the Dachshund displaced it in the most recent full-year AKC registration rankings. Through the early 2020s it held that position behind the French Bulldog, Labrador Retriever, Golden Retriever and German Shepherd Dog.
Part of the breed's standing on the list comes from how the AKC counts it. The club treats the Poodle as one breed with three varieties — Standard, Miniature and Toy — so registrations across all three sizes land on a single line. A buyer who takes home a six-pound Toy and a buyer who takes home a 60-pound Standard are registering the same breed.
The Poodle was developed in Germany as a water retriever and later refined in France, where it became the national dog. The sculpted show trim that looks purely ornamental today has a working origin: coat was left long over the chest and joints for warmth in cold water, and the hindquarters were clipped short to cut drag while swimming.
That dense, curly coat barely sheds, which is why the breed turns up on nearly every list of dogs suited to households sensitive to loose hair. The same coat is the breed's main upkeep. It mats without regular brushing and needs a professional trim roughly every four to six weeks, a recurring cost in both money and calendar time that shorter-coated breeds avoid.
The breed has a long competitive record in obedience, agility and dock diving. On health, Standard Poodles carry elevated risk of bloat, or gastric dilatation-volvulus, which can turn fatal within hours. Progressive$PGR +0.12% retinal atrophy, Addison's disease and sebaceous adenitis also appear in the breed.
One more factor sits outside the rankings entirely. The Poodle is the base for the doodle crossbreeds, and those dogs cannot be registered as purebred Poodles. Buyers who want that coat type without a purebred often choose a cross instead, and those puppies never reach the Poodle's registration total.

## Past No. 1 breeds show how much the rankings can shift over time
Credit: Canva Images
Only three breeds held the AKC's top spot in the five decades before the French Bulldog took it: the Poodle, the Cocker Spaniel and the Labrador Retriever. The Poodle led the registry through much of the 1960s and 1970s, the Cocker Spaniel took over in the 1980s, and the Labrador began its 31-year run in 1991.
Below No. 1, the list has churned much faster. The AKC's year-by-year rankings place both the Bulldog and the Beagle in the top five from 2013 through 2016, alongside the Labrador Retriever, the German Shepherd Dog and the Golden Retriever. Neither the French Bulldog nor the Dachshund appears anywhere in those lineups.
The Beagle shows how far a breed can slide without anything going wrong. A compact scent hound developed in England to hunt rabbit and hare, it held No. 4 or No. 5 through those mid-2010s years, then dropped out of the top five and has not returned.
The Bulldog's decline is more pointed, because it is a separate breed from the French Bulldog despite the shared name and flat-faced build. The Bulldog is heavier and broader — roughly 40 to 50 pounds against the French Bulldog's sub-28-pound frame — with an even shorter muzzle. It held a top-five position as late as 2020, and its exit tracks closely with the French Bulldog's climb, which points to buyers drawn to that look choosing the smaller, apartment-sized version.
The German Shepherd Dog ran the other way. It sat at No. 2 for most of the 2010s and now ranks No. 4 — movement, but within the narrow band it has occupied for decades.
Read as a buying guide, this history argues against treating rank as a verdict on quality. The Beagle and the Bulldog are the same breeds they were in 2014, judged against the same written standards. The registration volume around them changed.

**Dog breeds that have stayed inside the AKC’s top‑10 roster continuously from 2013 through 2024**

| Breed | Year‑by‑year presence (top‑10) |
|-------|--------------------------------|
| **Labrador Retriever** | #1 in 2013, 2014, 2015, … 2024 |
| **German Shepherd Dog** | #2 in 2013‑2017, 2020‑2024 (never dropped out of the top 10) |
| **Golden Retriever** | #3 throughout 2013‑2024 |
| **Poodle** | #8 in 2013, climbed to #5‑#6 in 2024 (continually top 10) |
| **Beagle** | #4‑#6 in 2013‑2017, still inside top 10 through 2024 |
| **English Bulldog** | #5 in 2013‑2019, #10 in 2020‑2024 (remained in the top 10) |
| **Rottweiler** | #9 in 2013, #8‑#9 in 2014‑2024 (always within the top 10) |

> **Why these breeds?**  
> 1. **Labrador Retriever, German Shepherd, Golden Retriever** are the “core‑4” breeds that have never fallen outside the last 10 spots during the 12‑year span.  
> 2. **Poodle, Beagle, English Bulldog, Rottweiler** have shown a persistent, year‑over‑year presence in the top 10, even as the ranks of other breeds have fluctuated.  
> 3. **French Bulldog** entered the top 10 in 2015 and is now (2024) the number‑1 breed, but it was **outside** the top 10 in 2013–2014, and thus does **not** qualify as a “consistent” top‑10 performer over the full 2013‑2024 window.
